utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-16-T the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sakic. I think that you are ready to answer the questions that I would still like to ask you today. Yesterday you spoke about the events of 20 October, 1992. I'm not going to ask you any questions about that part of your testimony. However, I would like to ask you a few questions about the period from 20 October, 1992 to 16 April, 1993, and after the questions we'll move to the events of 16 April, 1993. You told us, Mr. Sakic, that at the end of that day, that is the 20th of October, 1992, the Muslims who were living in Ahmici and Santici, or most of the Muslims in those cities, fled. They left, left their homes. Does that mean, as one might reasonably assume, that since they were conquered the Muslims were in fear for their security?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I said yesterday that the majority of the Muslim population from the lower part of Zume or the lower part of Ahmici, which is part of that region, Zume are hamlets, these are hamlets, not small towns, that it had moved deep -- deeper inside the village. I didn't claim that they were vanquished, defeated, because there was no fighting in that part. The shooting could be heard from the direction of the Catholic cemetery, at the place where the barricade was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Nonetheless, I seem to recall that you said that three or four days after these events, the events of 20 October, 1992, the Muslims came back to their homes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct I said that three or four days after the conflict, near the Catholic cemetery, all the citizens came back to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And you also told us that at the same time, that is three or four days after the events of 20 October, 1992, the Kupreskic families, who had left their homes, came back. Did I understand what you said, correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I said that at the same time that the Muslims came back to their homes the Kupreskic family, which was practically in the same part of the village, also came back to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: That means that the Kupreskic families were away from their homes for three or four days?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They came back together at the same time as the Muslims, so three or four days afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But why? Why did these families, these Croatian families, leave their homes for three or four days, which apparently the other Croatian families living in Ahmici and Santici did not do?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: The only families that were directly living in Ahmici were the Kupreskic families. The rest was a mixed population in lower Zume. They were bordering with the Muslim part. Since there was shooting, it's quite logical and understandable that both of them were afraid. I don't see anything unusual in that. Of course, after shooting you would be afraid to come back. These are bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, let's move to the negotiations that took place shortly afterwards, after the events of 20 October, 1992 that you spoke about, negotiations whose purpose was to re-establish peace and trust among the communities. You spoke about a meeting at the Ahmici school. You told us that you yourself were not present at the meeting, but that your father was. You told us that certain well-known Croatian people were there, and you mentioned Ivica Santic and Pero Skopljak. The Croats living in Ahmici, Santici and Pirici, were they represented during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: My father lives in Pirici, so he was there for sure, and then the majority of the neighbours were there also at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you know that Zoran Kupreskic participated in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say whether he did or did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Aside from your father, do you know the names of Croatians living in those villages who participated in the meeting at the Ahmici school?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I have to admit that I didn't really gather any information about that. I wasn't interested who was there when I was talking to my father; I was more interested in the end result. So I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let's speak about the results of that meeting. The principle result of the meeting, which was held for negotiations, was the return of the Muslims, that is all the Muslims, to their homes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No. At the time of the meeting the Muslims were already back in their homes, so the conversation -- the talk at the meeting, was to try to establish -- once again to re-establish trust and to alleviate these negative feelings that were beginning to happen during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understand. Yesterday, as an example, as an example of measures that were taken during that meeting, you mentioned assistance for reconstruction of the destroyed building on the 20th of October, 1992. Specifically I believe that you mentioned the home which belonged to Mehmed Ahmic. Can we say that that decision produced any results?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I can't confirm whether these events took place or not. One house was destroyed and then a few farm buildings, a couple of them on the Croat side and a couple on the Muslim side, but one house. I know that there was a decision made to repair the damage, and I even think that some help in construction materials was provided, but I can't be sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Were you informed about a decision taken by the Croatian community to -- to take weapons away from the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: First of all, I was only an inhabitant of the village. If such a decision did exist, I was not in the position to be informed about it or not to be informed about it, so I can't really answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When you spoke yesterday about the situation in Ahmici, Santici and Pirici, during that period following October of 1992 and which precedes the 16th of April, 1993, you spoke about a situation in which insecurity seemed to reign, and this was an increasing insecurity as time went by. It seemed to me that one of the reasons for that situation of insecurity was the issue of refugees. Have I correctly interpreted what you said?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I think that you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us that the Muslim refugees from the front area came to settle down in large numbers in Ahmici, whereas the Croatian refugees from the front area went to settle further away in other villages. As regards the situation, can we say that there was an imbalance that was a concern for the Croats?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I think that I said the following: After the fall of Jajce, which is a town 80 kilometres away from Vitez, it's not a village, there was a large migration of the population, so the entire Muslim and Croat population moved in the direction of Vitez. Apart -- some of these people, Muslims, remained in Vitez, some of them left for Zenica. A larger number, practically all of the Croats from Jajce, went towards the direction of Tomislavgrad and Herzegovina and a small number remained in Busovaca. This was a vast number of people on tractors, on horse-drawn carts, without any clear direction or aim. They were armed. So any such presence, that state of chaos, was a cause for insecurity. Also, the closeness of the Serb front line, which was 20 kilometres away from there, close to Travnik, was also a factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, I would like to move to the day of 15 April, 1993. Yesterday you told us that you came back from your work in Vitez between 6.00 and 7.00 in the evening. You told us that at that point, through your father you learned that Mr. Ivica Kupreskic's family was together, that mister -- that his wife was back after having been in Germany, and at that point you went to visit them. What were the relationships that you had with that family?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: My relations with the Kupreskic family were good, neighbourly. We grew up together. Some of us were younger, some were older. The husband, Ivica, is four or five years older than me. We used to play football together, we used to visit one another. Very good relations. Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But were you invited to go to visit them that evening?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: In Bosnia you don't have to be invited in order to visit. In Bosnia if you don't see a friend for a long time, you can go uninvited and he will greet you as if he had invited you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you go alone?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you know how Mrs. Kupreskic, that is Ivica Kupreskic's wife, came back from Germany?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I don't know the details, but I know approximately, and I can say that the children of Ivica Kupreskic came four days before the wife came to Vitez, and then Ivica came alone with his wife in a car. He came from Split to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us that the next day you were supposed to go to Grebak.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I was supposed to go to Grebak at 6.30 from Kaonik via Kresevo, Sarajevo, Trnovo to Grebak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: This is a question I want to ask because I don't know the answer: When one comes from Split to Ahmici by car, do you go past Grebak?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No. No, it's on the other side of the country and it's 300 kilometres away from there. It's approximately the distance between Split and Ahmici, and Ahmici to Grebak, only this is in the opposite direction. It's close to Goradze, which -- it's the Muslim enclave that was encircled. It was in the news a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Sakic, Mr. Ivica Kupreskic could give you no information about the condition of the roads going to Grebak?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, of course I didn't even ask him for that information, I was going to Grebak with the international committee, and only humanitarian vehicles could pass, no others could.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But if I ask you the question, it's because I seem to remember that yesterday you told us that you went to Mr. Ivica Kupreskic's house on that 15th of April, in the evening, in order to get some information about the situation, about the road conditions. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely right in what you just said. I wanted to get information about the road towards Split. It was the only road that was a civilian way out of Central Bosnia. It was a main road. So everybody was interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that on that evening, at Mr. Ivica Kupreskic's home, there were of course Mr. Ivica Kupreskic and his wife, yourself, Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, as well as two other individuals, Miroslav Pudza and Miro Vidovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes. I also think -- I think I mentioned Dragan Vidovic; Stipan. I think that he was there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Are you sure that you haven't forgot anybody?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure. Of course, it's possible that I did forget someone; that was seven years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understand. Are you sure that all the individuals that you mentioned were present?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether the wives of these men that you mentioned were present as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No. At the time that I was there, only Mrs. Kupreskic was there, Ivica's wife, Ankica Kupreskic. She brought us a bottle to drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: As regards these meetings in which there were almost only men, could we say that that's a rather generalised custom? Or does that correspond to a specific event?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't call it a meeting. I didn't come to an agreed meeting. I came there after I had heard that Mr. Kupreskic, Ivica, had arrived from Germany. And there I met his cousins, who were probably there for a while, and neighbours. So it didn't have any particular kind of form, or could have had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm wrong to ask this question, but it did seem to me that since you were celebrating Mrs. Kupreskic's return, who had been away for over a month -- actually more than a year -- the wives, his friends, might have been present as well.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, if it was a celebration, yes, but this was more of an informational kind of thing. The woman had arrived only a couple of hours before that, and we had come to see her. So I don't see anything unusual in that, in a good neighbourly atmosphere, and it's a normal thing in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understand. You told us that you spoke about the situation, the day's news and the kidnapping of Commander Totic. Among yourselves, could we say that the idea of tension, significant tension, during that day, was there, was an issue?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, up until about 6.00 I was in Vitez, at work. And I was getting ready to go to Grebak the next day. So I heard the information in Vitez. I can't describe the tension. It's not tangible to me. But you could sense the tension. That evening, when we were talking, we didn't have any information based on which we could come to any kind of conclusion. So it was -- I more or less came to see them, to talk a little bit with him. We touched on this briefly, and then I just turned around and I went back. So I spent an hour or two there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You said that you came back around 10.00 in the evening; did the others remain after you had left?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I left first, so I don't know how long the others stayed. But I know that I left at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore, as far as you can remember, Vlatko Kupreskic remained after you had left?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I think that they probably could have stayed, but I can't confirm 100 per cent. It's possible that they did, and it's possible that they didn't. At the time, I didn't know that it would be something that I would have to talk about later, so I can't remember all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: It's just out of curiosity that I'm asking you the question, but I see open in front of you a kind of a log or a handwritten book of some type. I'm not asking you to show us the notebook, because you don't use it during your testimony; but is that a diary that you kept during the events?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, if you wish, I'm prepared to give you that page, the page that I'm looking at. I will give it to you right away, and it can be translated. It's just a little summary containing dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: During your testimony yesterday, you told us that your father woke you up around 4.30; that you thought that it was a false alarm. Isn't it a bit strange to think about a false alarm, insofar as there was the precedent of the 20th of October 1992, and especially the idea of tangible -- almost tangible and growing tension that you mentioned in respect of the day of April 15th; that is, the day before?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, the alarms were an everyday occurrence, unfortunately, and they had been going on from the first, Serb strikes against us during the entire year. So really we didn't take them all that seriously later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did your father tell you who and under what circumstances he had this idea of an alert from?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me. Of course, he just rang the bell and said, "It seems to be an alarm of some kind, and it would be a good thing for you to come down." We didn't really go into it very much. Like I said before, it was an everyday occurrence -- not literally every day, but very often there were alarms, so it wasn't anything unusual for him to say that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understand. But perhaps you could tell us more specifically how these alarms or alerts were made known to the population.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, my father -- probably somebody else told my father, and he came. I can't really tell you. It's possible, but I don't know. I know only what he told me, and I didn't really pass that on further to anybody in order to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: However, it seems to me that you could tell us whether your father had been informed by telephone or through a messenger.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No, I can't really say one way or the other. I would have to make it up. That was the least important thing that I wanted to ask him at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that after having been woken up by your father, you thought there was a false alarm. You left your family, that is your wife and your two daughters, you left them sleeping, and then you went down in front of the house where neighbours had gathered. When you went out, were you armed?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No. I have a son and a daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Your neighbours or some of the neighbours in front of your house, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What kind of weapon did you see on that morning?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: With whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, with those of your neighbours who were armed.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: The neighbours? Not all of them; they were not all armed. Some of them had an M-48 rifle. I had a Kalashnikov, like I said yesterday, but I only brought that down later. So they were armed with bad and outdated firearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us that around 5.00, you saw first Zoran Kupreskic and his family going by -- that is, his wife and children -- then Mirjan Kupreskic and his family, and his mother-in-law as well. You told us that they went by your house, and they were moving toward Zume. But you also told us that your house was considered as a kind of safe shelter should there be any difficulties. Why were the families of Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic -- why did they not stop in front of your house in order to seek shelter?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: This shelter at my place, that's where the neighbours who lived in the four or five houses in the neighbourhood sought shelter. It's a basement covering an area of about 16 square metres, and not many people could really fit in. They probably knew about that, and also they didn't come there before when there were alarms, alerts, and that is probably the reason why they didn't stop, why they went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Does that mean that there was an organisation among the Croats in Ahmici, Santici, and Pirici, and that each family knew which shelter it should go to?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't put it that way. As I said yesterday, the depression by our house was showed on maps in the former system as a place where people were to seek shelter when greater masses of people and civilians were on the move. I wouldn't say that this was a specially elaborated plan. We simply knew, after this large number of alarms and alerts, where we should all seek shelter. As I said, we had been trained, so to speak, because of the Serb attacks, the aviation attacks, there were so many from the beginning of the year, so we all knew which way to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Five or ten minutes after the Kupreskic families had gone by moving toward Zume, you saw coming from Zume, at least from the direction of Zume, a group of soldiers whom you described as being heavily armed and you told us that probably they belonged to a unit of the military police of the HVO. I would merely like, further to your description, to ask you whether you noticed whether any of the soldiers had a coloured ribbon on their shoulders: That is, red, blue, or white, or orange, or yellow.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yesterday, in my statement, I said that on their shoulders they had a light ribbon. I don't know if it was white or blue, but it was very light. It was dark, so I couldn't exactly tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When the soldiers went by your house, where exactly were you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Do you want me to show this to you on the map? On the road in front of my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We have in our minds the photographs that were given to the Tribunal yesterday that are now D92/ -- I know that the house was facing the road and behind it was a garage and behind the garage was the depression. When the soldiers went by your garage, were you in front of your house, between your house and the road?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I'd like to show this on the map. This would be easier for everyone to understand that way. I was approximately 25 metres towards Zume, or 30 metres. It's on the map. It's shown very nicely on the map, so perhaps it would be more concise if I simply showed it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, could we give D92/2 to the witness? Mr. Sakic, if we look at photograph number 1, is it correct to say that the facade where you can see the balconies face the road, and, therefore, face southwest?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No. It doesn't face the road. The entrance -- the middle of the house, that is the one that faces the road. That is to say, the direction of Zume. And the front part of the facade with the two terraces, it faces an internal part that goes into the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore, on photograph 1, one cannot see the road that the soldiers took.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: You can, of course. It's only 20 metres long; right? Of course you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could we put photograph number 1 on the ELMO so that the witness can show us where the road was in relation to his house? Mr. Sakic, on photograph number 1 which is on the ELMO, could you show us exactly where the road goes by your house?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Of course I can, but I'm a technical person. We're doing this the wrong way. It's easier to show it on the map, and it's better to put it in context by showing it on the map. I can show it to you on the photograph too --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would the witness listen? Would you kindly just answer the questions that counsel is putting, rather than arguing with him? Now, he's asking you to do something and show us something on the photograph. Would you kindly do that, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: This is where the road is, where the soldiers passed (indicating). It goes from the garage towards here, about 30 metres this side, and there's a small crossroads here, and this is where the entrance to my house is, from this road (indicating). So here from the garage there is a path leading that way to the crossroads, and then from the crossroads here to the house (indicating). And that's why I thought it was better to show it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I think we understood these explanations very clearly, the explanations that you've given us. Could you show us now, on photograph number 1, the location where you were when the soldiers went by on the road?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I cannot show it. Here on the crossroads, the one that you can not see on the photograph, it's here, about 15 metres approximately from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. When the soldiers went by, did they stop to say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Since you speak the same language and you have the same nationality, did you ask them anything?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I indeed did not ask them anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Isn't that a little bit strange, because there was an alert, you were in front of your home with your neighbours, some of your neighbours took -- had taken their families to shelters, nothing is happening. You don't know anything at all, according to your statement, about what was going on or is about to happen. You saw soldiers but you asked them absolutely no information.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I must admit, from this advantage point here it seems a bit strange to me, but at that point, indeed, I did not ask them a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And none of the neighbours with whom you found yourself asked any questions either; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if they did. It seemed too dangerous. It seemed too dangerous, and we didn't really want to exhibit any unnecessary curiosity. I'm saying this from my very own point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And we'll take it as a very personal point of view. But if the situation was apparently so dangerous, why did you take no -- make no arrangements at that point to protect your family, which, if I understood correctly, was still sleeping on the upper floor of the home?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: You did not understand this well. My family went downstairs perhaps 20 minutes after I descended. So they went downstairs before 5.00, but they did not join me immediately. They didn't go downstairs exactly when I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let's go back to the group of soldiers passing in front your house. Yesterday you told us they moved toward the Kupreskic homes. You told us yesterday, I think, that they moved toward the Kupreskic homes, going through that depression. Have I -- did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, you did understand me correctly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Mr. Sakic, to show us, on the aerial photograph of Ahmici, the road that the soldiers were going along in order to go from your house to the Kupreskic house?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: This is where my house is (indicating). This is where the crossroads is, the one I mentioned a few minutes ago (indicating). This is a forest which is naturally higher, and this is a depression, and the soldiers took the lower part of the forest, so that is to say they went below the forest to the Kupreskic houses (indicating). This is the path they took.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In order to get into the depression, did the soldiers go by your garage? Excuse me. This was my question: In order to go down into the depression and to join up with the Kupreskic houses, did the soldiers go near your -- or, rather, did they pass near your garage?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You may be seated. Let's say a few things about this depression. If I understood correctly, this was a kind of a ground which had crumbled in, where formerly there had been a mine.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Partly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, that's not a very important detail. Yesterday you told us that this depression was used in the former Yugoslavia as a refuge for villages in cases of fires?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Actually, there are two depressions. The soldiers took the one below, underneath the forest, as I showed you on the map a few minutes ago. They went straight on, and the depression on the left-hand side was the one where, in the times of the former Yugoslavia, we -- we have this -- what should I call it -- place where we could seek refuge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I'm asking you to give D85/2, 85/2, which was tendered in evidence yesterday. Mr. Sakic, what I'm interested in for right now is the road that the soldiers went along going from your house to the Kupreskic houses. When you look at these photographs, and specifically let me call your attention to photographs number 8 and 11, can one see and reconstitute the road that the soldiers took?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Part of the road, yes. On photograph number 11 one can see part of the road. On photograph number 8 that's not it. It is quite the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore, the soldiers went down into the depression through the access that you can see on photograph number 11?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: On one of the photographs can one see the location where they would have -- from which they would have access to the Kupreskic house? Would that be photograph number 7, for example?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: On photograph number 7 it is quite the opposite, like photograph number 8, in terms of the road which they took. On photograph number 11, by this tree, I can show it over here too, you can see the road they took. They went straight ahead, they did not turn left by the tree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The houses that you see on photographs 7 and 8, you can see a group of houses, two or three at least. Aren't they the Kupreskic houses?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No. No, these are not the Kupreskic houses. On photograph number 7 is a farm building owned by Ivo Kupreskic, and you can only see the top and a new farm building that was not there at the time of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you show us, Mr. Sakic, so that we understand things well, on the aerial photograph could you show us exactly where the house that we see in photographs 7 and 8, at least one of the two -- of those houses which was in existence at the time? Could you show that to us on the aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I shall start once again from my garage. The soldiers took the lower depression by the garage, straight ahead, that is to say, underneath the forest toward the Kupreskic houses and Ahmici (indicating). The depression from which the picture of the house was taken goes to the left, and that is to say that those buildings that are on the photographs 7 and 8, if I'm not mistaken, are there, are over here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understand. It's the house which is a little bit above the houses occupied by the Kupreskic family.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I was saying that the house that you showed us is a house which actually is a little bit above the houses in which the Kupreskic family lived.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Approximately in a straight line from Ivo Kupreskic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, can we say that when you come from Zume and you go in the direction of the houses that the Kupreskic family lived in, the most natural road, the most direct road and the fastest road, was to move by going into the depression near your garage and then to follow the depression until you reach the Kupreskic houses?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: One could say the following: Both our paths, pedestrian paths, the lower one and the upper one too, they were mostly taken by children when they went to school and adults when they went to the cemetery. So these were pedestrian paths. And the road that one can take by car ends at my garage, so only these pedestrian paths go on from there. The upper part is more directly leading towards the Kupreskic houses and the other one goes around a bit, and they probably -- these soldiers, they did not have to take paths and roads, they could move through forests and fields as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The fact that they used that road does show that they were very familiar with that part of Ahmici, Santici and Pirici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Obviously they were familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You mentioned the names of the people -- of those people with whom you spent part of that day, or spent the day specifically in that depression, but I see that you didn't speak about your brother.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I didn't mention my brother. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Where was your brother?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: From the beginning of 1992, my brother was in the anti-aircraft defence. That is to say that he was at three or four places around Vitez. That is where these anti-aircraft guns were placed. He was a reserve officer from the former Yugoslavia in the anti-aircraft defence, and he also had regular tours of duty there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did he live in the same house as you did?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No. No. He had a house of his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What's his first name, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Slavko Sakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: He was born in 1961; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you see him on that day in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No. That day he was in Vitez, that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: In the evening my sister-in-law, Jasna, his wife, told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What contact did you have with your sister-in-law?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: What kind of a relationship I had? I had a normal relationship, like any brother-in-law living next door. And she was there in the shelter. I mentioned her.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Sakic. What I was asking was that the following: You said that -- if I understood you correctly, you said that on the evening of the 16th of April, you learned from your sister-in-law that your brother Slavko was in Vitez. I want to know how you learned that. How did that information get to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Oh, I really don't know. Perhaps we talked at home. I don't know. It's quite customary over there at our place to have a cup of coffee, talk. I simply don't know. Slavko had been going on this duty for a year already, and he stopped working at the factory, and all these people who were in the PZO had already been mobilised. It was a routine thing. There was nothing unusual about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Was he still living in Pirici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Slavko lives in Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What do you say about the following fact: On the 26th of September, 1998, in this Tribunal, a witness who testified under the pseudonym "X" said that he had seen, on the 16th of April, 1993, your brother, Slavko, wearing a uniform, with other soldiers near the Kupreskic houses.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I don't know how he could have seen that, honestly. At that time my brother certainly was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic were dressed that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Zoran Kupreskic? I'll try to remember. I think that he might have been wearing black trousers, and what was characteristic was a big jacket that he had. It was at least two sizes too big for him and it was unbuttoned, and he had a sweater. I think he could have had a sweater underneath that jacket. And some kind of ankle-high shoes, boots. That was it, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The description is the one you've got for Mirjan?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I remember Mirjan Kupreskic by an unusual detail. He had woollen socks, knee high. He was always sickly, and his mother always made him dress properly, and I don't think that he could have had any kind of camouflage jacket. I think that he had civilian clothes. I think that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What colour were the clothes that Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic were wearing?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say that with certainty now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, if you don't remember, just tell me that you don't.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic were -- had a weapon?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Mirjan Kupreskic had a rifle, I think, an old M-48, and Zoran, I think, had a shotgun. I found out later that day that he got it from his cousin, Ivica Kupreskic. It was a hunting gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yesterday, during your testimony, you told us that you spent part of the day in the depression that we spoke about a few minutes ago. I don't really understand the explanations that you gave yesterday about the fact that you were in the depression. In what way could the depression serve as a shelter?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I said before that the depression was a natural shelter. It is very close to my house, practically begins. The path goes down towards the depression from my garage, and then it goes to the right towards the Kupreskic houses and towards Ahmici. So it was quite logical that we go there. I can't explain now. It was just logical for us to be there, it's as simple as that. That's where we were sheltered from everything. We were close to the first shelter, where several families were, in my house, and that's where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You said that you were sheltered from everything in that depression; however, you were not sheltered from mortar shells. And yesterday you said that a shell fell near the place where you were.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes. The depression could only be penetrated by a mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Excuse me, but I'm trying to go back to the logic that you used yesterday: Wouldn't it have been logical, since there was a danger that mortar shells might fall on that depression, would it be logical for you to withdraw to a shelter which would have a kind of a concrete covering over it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: In view of the fact that this was only one mortar shell, there weren't more than that one, we thought that it was not necessary for us to move from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Very well. Yesterday you told us that the first shots began around 5.30, and that about 15 minutes later -- that is, about 5.45 -- you saw the light from the first fires, the glow of the first fires. Am I correct in respect of those details?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us that the smoke or that the glow of the first fires was coming from the direction of the Kupreskic houses, but that you could not see from where you were which house was in the process of burning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I said that the firing was coming from several directions. The place where we were, the first team (sic) that we saw -- the first smoke that we saw was from the direction of the Kupreskic houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But you said that particularly from where you were, you could not see what house was burning?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Might one not be surprised by the fact that Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic apparently did not feel the need to go to see what was happening, particularly if it was their house or another house that was burning?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, as I mentioned, the firing was so strong, and you could hear the sounds of the bullets; they were whizzing through the air so much that we couldn't even raise our heads up, because we had no military experience at all. Shortly before that, a mortar shell fell close to us, so that we were frozen to the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understand. But during that morning of the 16th of April, wasn't there a lull during which Zoran or Mirjan, or both of them, could have gone to see whether their houses had been hit or not?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: There was no lull, absolutely. I think the firing was escalating. It was growing stronger throughout the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore there was no moment during that day of the 16th of April when it was possible, without risking one's life, to see clearly what was going on with the Kupreskics' house?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I don't think it was possible. Maybe for somebody it was possible, but in view of our inexperience and our fear, the first -- this was the first shooting that we had experienced on that day, and it was happening around us. So in view of the fear that we felt, we could not have gone to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, when you say that someone else might have been able to, when you say someone else might have, who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I mean those who were shooting, of course, if they are shooting, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: During that morning, at around 9.00 or 10.00, you went to Zume with Zoran and Mirjan to see whether the people who had taken shelter were all right; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Between 9 and 10.00 we came from the depression; then we went down to the shelter in my house. After that, we went along the road towards Zume to see how their families were doing. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: At any point during that morning, on the Zume road, did you run into Vlatko -- Vlatko Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: (No translation given)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You mentioned another incident then that was your meeting with Nikola Omazic, and you said that Nikola Omazic was a neighbour, he was a little bit drunk, and he told you that Mirjan Santic had been killed near the Kupreskic houses. Was he a soldier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Just for the record, for the record, because when you asked "At any point during that morning, on the Zume road, did you run into Vlatko Kupreskic?" He said no, to the best of my recollection, he said no, and here it doesn't appear on the record. So there is no answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: He said no, he didn't meet Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, let's speak about that person, Nikola Omazic. You told me that it was a neighbour, he was a little bit drunk, and that he told you that Mirjan Santic had been killed, and had been killed near the Kupreskic houses. My question was the following: Was Nikola Omazic a soldier?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Was he wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I don't think that he was wearing a uniform. I don't think so. But I can't say it with certainty. He could have been -- have had a part; nobody there had a whole uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Was he armed?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Having -- wearing part of a uniform, with a weapon, near the Kupreskic houses, where you just said it was very dangerous to be, how could one not think that it was not a soldier?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I saw Nikola Omazic that morning at my house, and then when I came back from Zume, I saw him next to my garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Perhaps you were near your garage at one point or another in the day, but these locations are very close to one another. I wanted to ask the following question: Were you really sure that that day that Nikola Omazic was not a soldier?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: On that day, Nikola Omazic was just like the rest of us civilians. He was armed, as I said; he was there next to the garage. He was together with Dragan Vidovic -- Ivica Kupreskic first, then Dragan Vidovic, Stipe, Mirjan Kupreskic, and Zoran Kupreskic. They brought Mirjan Santic down to my garage; then Mirjan's body was taken by his parents. I think Nikola Omazic possibly went with them in the direction of Zume. I'm absolutely sure that he was not a soldier that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, with the assistance of the usher, I'm going to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number 354.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, Nikola Omazic, who is the son of Ante, who was born in 1958 in Ahmici, is that the person that we're speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You can see in the document that -- under the signature of Mario Cerkez, you can see that Nikola Omazic was wounded on the 16th of April, 1993, in Pirici, whereas -- while he was fighting with the Muslims, and that he was carrying out the combat orders that had been given to him by the appropriate authority.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I can confirm that Nikola Omazic was there, as I confirmed in my earlier testimony. I can also confirm that in the late afternoon hours, he was wounded, because as I had said before, he was slightly drunk; so probably this was a consequence -- the fact that he was drunk and not careful was the reason why he was wounded. But I found out the next day that he was wounded. I didn't know that on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And in light of this document, might one not think that Nikola Omazic was a soldier who had had a bit too much to drink?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if you would think that based on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mightn't one think, when we look at this same document, that on that day he was a soldier who was under the command of the Vitez Brigade, and not the military police unit?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the hierarchical structure. During that first day, when I saw Nikola Omazic, he was not wearing any kind of army uniform, and I don't know if he was in a unit or not. Later, because three days later I left, so it's quite possible, and I believe that after that he did become a member of some unit, because later everybody did become a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But from what you've just said, Mr. Sakic, couldn't one conclude that on that day in Ahmici there might have been soldiers there who were not wearing uniforms? That is, not all of them had to be wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, just the fact that he was wounded, based on that, I couldn't conclude that. Bullets were falling everywhere, and anyone could have been wounded, anybody who was not careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I don't think you've answered my question. I'm going to ask you a different question, a few questions about the death of Mirjan Santic. Yesterday we were given a death certificate that had been issued by the appropriate authority of the Bosnian Croat government, and it was given to the Tribunal as D86/2. Apparently on -- we can see on that official document, which is a death certificate, that the death of Mirjan Santic took place on the 17th of April in Santici.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, I'm absolutely sure that Mirjan Santic was killed on the first day of the conflict, close to the houses of Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Once again I'm going to ask the usher to give you a document; this is Prosecution 337. As you can see on the first page of the document, it's a document called "List of members of the HVO who were killed," which has the date 24 February, 1994, and which has been classified as strictly military secrets, strictly confidential. Would you please look at the -- 445. I made a mistake; excuse me, Your Honour. 435.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, did you find the order number 435?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could we not consider, when we read this document, that Mirjan Santic died on the 18th of April -- the year on the original is illegible; we assume that it was 1993 -- in Santici? 18 April, and not 16 April?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, I can say the following: Mirjan Santic was killed for sure on the first day of the conflict. I'm absolutely sure. Here it is also undoubtedly written that he was killed or that he was buried a day or two later, here on this paper. But I am absolutely sure that he was killed on the first day, because that was the first dead person that I had ever seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Excuse me, but the date is not indicated on the document, of the burial.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, you said the 18th, and here -- I can hardly see it on that copy, but it's possible that it says the 18th of April. Yes, that's what it said, the 18th of April. I'm talking about the killing: He was killed on the first day of the conflict, the 16th. And the document -- well, it's clear here, it states clearly the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How can one explain, if we're only speaking about this document, that there were two documents, both of which were official; one gives the date of 16th of April, the other one 18th of April? And in order to find the date of the 16th, which would confirm your testimony, we have only an indication in a book which was published by the Ministry of the Interior of the Croatian Community, about which one might think -- I'll ask you for your opinion: One could consider this to be a propaganda tool that was used for the special unit that was represented by the military police?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, would you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I was saying, Mr. Sakic, that we have two documents, both of which are official, and neither mentions the date of 16 April as being the date of Mirjan Santic's death. I'm not referring to your testimony now. To certify the date of 16 April as being the date of his death, we have only a book that was published by the Ministry of the Interior of the Croatian community in April 1995, if I remember correctly, about which one might think that it is a propaganda book which could be used for a special unit of the HVO, which was the military police. This comment, which is more a comment than a question, does that call for any comments from you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, listen. As I said earlier, Mirjan was killed on the 16th. Why one -- certain documents say that this happened on the 17th or the 18th, I really don't know. So that can be my only comment regarding this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: On the same document that you have in front of you, please look at number 96. Now I'm asking you a question, and this has to do with number 96. We see the number of Ivanovic (sic), Jure Slavko. Yesterday you spoke about the death of a person named Slavko Ivanovic (sic) -- or Ivankovic. Is that the same person?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I didn't say that yesterday. Yesterday I said that Zlatko Ivankovic was killed, the son of Ilija Ivankovic, and that his father was working in the same company that I worked at, and that Zlatko worked through the youth employment agency in my company, but I did not remember Slavko Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Please look at 481. This person, Ivica Zepackic, the son of Stipica, is that the person that we were speaking about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I said yesterday that I -- I know personally Zlatko Ivankovic, son of Ilija. He is the -- Slatko, son of Ilija Ivankovic, and I know for certain that he was killed on the first day of the conflict, together with a person named Zepackic, whom I don't know. So based on this I don't know whether that was the same Zepackic, but I know for sure that he was killed together, on the first day of the conflict, at the Catholic cemetery with Zlatko Ivankovic. That's what I heard from Zlatko's father.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: However, yesterday the Trial Chamber was given a death certificate in the name of Ivica Zepackic, and on the list we see the same Ivica Zepackic who died at a date which is -- on a date which is illegible, but who did die not in Ahmici or Santici but in Kruscica, and who was not a member of the military police but of the Vitezovi. Would you like to comment about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, I can only confirm the following: That in the direction of the cemetery on the first day of the conflict, Ivankovic Zlatko and Zepackic were killed for sure, whom I don't know. I can absolutely confirm that they died on the first day in the morning, which I found out from Zlatko Ivankovic's father.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: A final question, Your Honour, and then I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecutor is giving the witness the name of a person who was killed that has nothing to do with the name of the person who was killed that the witness mentioned yesterday, because if the book on the military police and the members of the military police who were killed, you could see that these are two different persons, that this is a different person from the one that the Prosecutor is asking about. So for the person that the Prosecutor is asking the questions about, it's possible that that is so, but that is not the same person that the witness is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I don't understand. In this document you're talking about Ivica Zepackic, and you see the same name on the list, 481. I have the impression that it's the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: It is a person who, in fact, was mentioned only by his family name but not by his first name by the witness, that is. Then Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac presented a death certificate under the name of Ivica Zepackic, a document which was tendered in evidence as D88/2, and my question was to know whether that was the same person whose name is on the list of the HVO members who were killed during the conflict. Of course, the Judges must evaluate each of the documents submitted to them, must evaluate them according to their correct weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: My final question, Mr. Sakic is the following one: You tell us that during that day, the day of 16th of April, 1993, in Ahmici, the three members of the Croatian forces died. Do you know how many Muslims died on that same day in Ahmici -- in Santici, Ahmici and Pirici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I said before that I think five Croats were killed in that conflict. Unfortunately, many more Muslims were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, as regards the two other Croats who were mentioned yesterday, from the documents themselves which Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac showed, the documents show us, from the statements that you made yesterday, that three Croats, as far as you know and according to what you've said, died on the 16th of April in Ahmici. So here's my question: How --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise for just a moment. Mr. Terrier is not saying correctly. He had heard that five -- the witness had heard that five Croats were killed in Ahmici on that day. So I would like for Mr. Terrier to cite back the witness's statements from yesterday correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac, I have my own notes, and according to the witness two Croats were killed on the 16th, one in Ahmici and one in Santici. Two Croats. Mirjan Santic and Zlatko Ivankovic. And then three died in Vitez, three Croats in Vitez, and that's confirmed by the documents that you tendered. Therefore, these are people who died in Vitez. Mr. Terrier, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness, in fact, did say, as you recalled -- all I have to do is look at the transcript, that there is no ambiguity in the transcript in that respect -- that as far as he knows, five Croats died in Ahmici on that day, but the documents that had been given to the Tribunal by Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac, it shows that two of the Croats had died in Vitez and not in Ahmici. Therefore, in principle, my question does not relate to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You said that three or five Croats died in Ahmici. My question is: Do you know how many Muslims, on that same day, were killed in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. Of course, I know there were a lot of people, more than 60, for sure. Later I heard that it was about a hundred, but I heard this later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you know how many Croat homes were destroyed in Ahmici on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I think that there were no destroyed Croatian homes in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you know how many Muslim houses were destroyed on that day in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I don't know how many were destroyed in Ahmici on that day, but later I know for sure that all the houses were destroyed in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, can one honestly say, as one said yesterday, talk about fate or accidents?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, I can talk about myself and my friends who happened to be there, and I would say that the only misfortune of those people, of us who were neighbours and did not take part in that, is the fact that we were born there. We could not have any influence on what was happening. It was beyond our control. I can say that. I can also say that what happened was not good, but from the position where I was then, where I was living and from what I was doing as my work, I could not, myself or any of my friends, have any influence on the course of events. And we cannot, in any way, none of us, be responsible because we had just been born there. We were not able to choose that. We were there, crimes were committed. We did not commit them, none of my friends. Without doubt, a crime was committed and the perpetrators should be found, because that's the only way to help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have any further questions. I would like to tender as evidence 354 and document called "Three Years of Military Police," In the Croatian version and in English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is number 355.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objections from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. They are admitted into evidence. All right. I think we should now -- it's high time for us to take a break, so a 30-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 10.10 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic -- actually, could we first ask the usher to give the witness this document, Prosecutor's document, and this shows who belonged to what unit and who was wounded. Number 354. Mr. Sakic, can you see in this document from when Nikola Omazic belonged to the Vitez Brigade, was a member of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: It says in this document that Nikola Ante Omazic, born in 1958, was a member of the HVO or the Vitez Brigade from the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you also see the date when this document was issued on the top of there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: The date is the 27th of June, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether on that day, the 16th of April, you saw when, in which way, and where Nikola Omazic was mobilised or included in HVO units?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So did you see some other members of the village guards, or rather people who were together with you, were in any contact with officials from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Had this been the case, I would have had to have been on one of the lists too, as I was there. It is certain that no one made any kind of list of that kind at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Please, could you have a look at the text, where it is mentioned that this person, Nikola Omazic, was wounded by a sniper. Tell me, was it possible to wound a person by sniper shot, a person who was in Pirici or Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: It was absolutely possible to be wounded by any kind of bullet, a straying bullet, any bullet -- I mean, one cannot tell whether it was a sniper shot. I don't see how it could be said that he was wounded by a sniper shot. He was wounded by a bullet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was there any shooting in the area of Pirici? Could you tell us that once again, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: There was shooting all over that day, and it was practically constant.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Please, could you have a look at these photograph files?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher to hand them out.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D94/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, could you tell us what you can see on photograph number 1.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: On photograph number 1, we can see part of the garage and my woodshed, that belonging to me and to my father, as well as part of the entrance into the depression leading to the Kupreskics'.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you show us where this road goes, what direction? Towards the Kupreskic houses, I mean; can you show that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I can show the direction, approximately, because I know where it leads. Yes, I can show it on this photograph too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you use a marker and show the direction?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: (Indicating) This is the direction towards the Kupreskics'.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Is that the direction in which the unit that you saw went?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No, the unit went in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. Could you tell me, on the second photograph, what can you see on the second photograph? Whose houses are these?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: On the second photograph, we can see the view from the garage towards Zume. And on the left-hand side -- you can't really see this very well -- on the left-hand side are the Pudza houses. Then this is Brnada Ante's house, and this road leads to Zume. That is the road from the direction from which they came.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So the soldiers came from that direction along that road; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, from Zume.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Please have a look at photograph number 3. And what can you see there? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Photograph number 3 shows the same direction, but it was taken closer up. It was taken from the crossroads where this small path leads to my house. That is to say, approximately, it is about 80 metres away from the garage -- this picture, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You mean the place from which the picture was taken; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Please, photograph number 4 now.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Photograph number 4 shows the following crossroads, and this is part of the road that deviates and goes to Nikola Omazic's house. That is to say that on the right-hand side is Nikola Omazic's house, and this is a house of a man called Brnadaman (phoen), who lives in Sweden and works there; his father was there, I think. And on the left-hand side is the house of Brnad Gabriel (phoen), and that is where his son Anto lives. And this is Samija Ljuba's house, and it's unfinished, and I think he lives in Austria.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This picture, is that a bit further away, further along this road?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, this is further along, in relation to the previous photograph, of course, and now it shows another direction towards Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And these houses on the right-hand side, on photographs 2, 3, and 4, all of that is the same house, isn't it, just from different directions?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: On Photograph Number 2, and on photograph number 4 is one and the same house. And Number 2, Number 4 -- no, not number 3. That is the house of Ante Brnada. So that is to say on pictures 4 and 2, this house is the same one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just have a look at Photograph Number 5 as well, please, and is this a continuation of that road?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Photograph Number 5 was taken from this crossroads, and it goes further on towards Zume, towards the house of Milan Samir, and it was taken from Slavko Pudza's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That is to say that this road leads to your house?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: This was taken from the direction of Zume, and in the opposite direction it leads to my house, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And now, please, could you mark on this map --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President? So that we understand the testimony correctly, wouldn't it be useful to look on photograph 1 particularly, to have the witness show us with a felt-tipped pen what the road was that they took? Because he said that on photograph 1, he said that this was the road that the soldiers took in order to go to the depression. I think he might able to mark it with a felt pen or with an arrow of some sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we ask the witness to do what the Prosecutor just asked. That is, on photograph number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: The direction in which the soldiers moved was as follows (Indicating), and the depression where the Kupreskics are is in this direction. That is to say behind the garage, towards the depression; that's where they went. And this is the left-hand depression that leads to the Kupreskic houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Please, could you mark the direction in which the soldiers moved by "A," or "1," and would you mark the direction in which the Kupreskic houses are with a "B. "

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, so that we understand "B", the "B" that is on the photograph was actually behind the house.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Are you referring to photograph number 1? That of course is behind the house, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Please, on this aerial photograph --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D95/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, could you please put a circle around your own house on this aerial photograph with a marker, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you show the road from which you saw this unit coming? Could you please mark the road that you saw, the road that you can see now where you saw them coming? You can also put an arrow in the direction in which they were moving.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And now could you mark the road that these soldiers took as they were leaving.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And would you mark that direction with the letter "A," please.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you mark the road that Zoran Kupreskic and Mirjan Kupreskic took as they came to your house, or rather as they came to this road.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And mark it with the letter "B," please.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Those are the two pedestrian paths at the same time, are they?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, they are. Yes, they are; both of them are pedestrian paths.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just one more thing, please: Could you just show where the entrance door of your house is? Which side does it face?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: There are two doors. There is one here that faces this road, that is to say toward the Pudza houses, and the direction in which they came.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And where is the door and the shelter on that side -- on which side is that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Here (Indicating). Here, on the south, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: They face the Vitez/Busovaca road; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, the Vitez/Busovaca road.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just one more thing. Could you please put a circle around the building that can be seen in the photo file that we showed you, that is to say, those two houses on the -- in the photo file of the depression? You said that these are farm buildings, that one was built later and one existed at the time of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Please, one more thing. Could you just mark on the aerial photograph where the crossroads is, the one that leads to the house of Mira Samija and Mirko Vidovic that we have in the first photo file. Can you see it there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Practically there are two roads leading to Mira Samija's house. This is this one (marks).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you please mark the crossroads that we can see on photograph number 3?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: On photograph number 3? It is this crossroads here (marks).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just put an "X" here.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Also, I would like to ask you, in connection with photograph number 1, can you mark the place where you stood that morning? Can we see here the place you stood when the soldiers were passing by, that is to say, where you encountered the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: You cannot see it on this photograph. It's about 20 metres in front of the garage, that is to say, in this direction at the crossroads, where the road forks off toward the front part of my house, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about the conflict on the 20th of October, '92? When did you see Muslims fleeing? When were they leaving the village, do you remember? What was the time of day?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I think they were fleeing in the course of the entire day. I can't remember exactly, but I think it was throughout the day. The first time that I saw them was in the afternoon, on the road that was going beneath my house, in the direction of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At that time were -- was the fighting still going on or had it stopped?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I think you could still hear shooting at that time. It stopped in the late afternoon, I can't remember exactly when, but you could still hear the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
