utterances.text: Could you please tell us if you know how many children, at that time, at the end of '92, did Mirjan Kupreskic and Zoran Kupreskic have, and how old were those children?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Zoran Kupreskic at the time had three sons. He still has three sons. The oldest was going to school with my daughter. The youngest was maybe about a year old, and the middle son was maybe about two or three. I can't remember exactly. Mirjan Kupreskic had a daughter who was about four years old at the time, and then another smaller child. I think that child was less than a year old.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did the family of Ivica Kupreskic, during the first conflict, stay in their house in Pirici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Ivica Kupreskic's family was abroad. They were in Germany. They were staying with Ivica's brother Branko. They were refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did the family of Branko Kupreskic stay in Pirici at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Branko Kupreskic's family was also in Germany, just as the family of Jozo Kupreskic was. He was Ivica's brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So this is Jozo or Josip?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, Josip. His nickname is Jozo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So those three families of Branko, Josip and Ivica Kupreskic were away during the first conflict in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes. They were away. Branko was permanently residing there; he lives and works there. The others went shortly after the first Serb strikes, when a lot of the population went abroad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So in the region where the Kupreskic houses were, which families were there at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: At the time Zoran Kupreskic with his family, Mirjan Kupreskic with his family, and Mirjan and Zoran's father, with his wife, they were all at the Kupreskic houses, and an old aunt of theirs. I think it was Ivica Kupreskic's aunt. And there was nobody else there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know if during the second conflict Branko Kupreskic and Josip Kupreskic were in Pirici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No. At the time of the second conflict, or shortly before the second conflict, Ivica Kupreskic had come back. He brought his wife and children. Branko and Josip remained living and working in Germany. Branko is still in Germany, and Josip came back just recently.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you said that in that region during the first conflict, only the families of Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic were there, and one of their aunts and their mother and father?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, their mother and father too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did anybody else besides them have any small children? Were there any small children there except for the five small Kupreskic children?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, not at their houses, but in other places, yes, of course there were. We all had children.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I'm only talking about this part. The Prosecutor asked you if you had -- or who told you about the conflict, the possibility that a conflict may break out, and you've said that you were informed by your father when he woke you up, and that he wasn't very definite?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You also said that you didn't know and you didn't even ask who had informed your father.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was there any talk at some other time with other people about the way in which they were informed, people who were there standing next to your house?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No, I didn't really talk. I stayed there for three days. On the fourth day I left that location. I went to Vitez, to the town, and a month and a half after that I left Vitez. So at that time it was the least important to know who informed who. It was really very -- it was unimportant at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This unit that you saw, could you indicate on the aerial photograph the exact place where you encountered them? Can that be indicated? Is that very close to your house?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, I could say, but I already marked that place with a marker, so if you have another map perhaps. It's very hard to see on this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would the usher please give the witness another map in order to indicate the place? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D96/2.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I will indicate the place where I first encountered this unit (marks). So exactly where this part of the road branches off, in front of my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you specify how far that place is from your house?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, I will try to specify that. About 25 to 30 metres at the most.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You can place the letter "A" there on that map, and also mark the place where you were in the depression for those three days.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: (Marks). We were in the upper part of the depression.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So would you please indicate that place with the letter "B"?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you encountered the unit, what did you think? You said yesterday that in a way you were frightened.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, of course I was frightened. It was early morning. It was still a little dark, and a group of armed men was approaching us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What were you afraid of? Were you afraid you were going to be attacked?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No, I wasn't afraid that we would be attacked, I was afraid -- well, at that time, as I said before, there was a constant feeling of fear, and it was quite a normal reaction for me to be frightened. I had no idea what was going on. That was a group of armed men approaching us under full military equipment, so we were afraid. Everybody who was there was afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was it usual to see at night, or in the morning or in the evening groups of well-armed men ready for action, with painted faces?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, in the terrain, in the area where I was living, I had never seen such a group of men who were armed and masked in such a way, camouflaged in such a way, it was the first time, and I really thought that this only happened on the front.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was there any kind of street lighting in your village?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes -- no, no. There was no street lighting in the village at that time, and there isn't any lighting now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At that time, at around 5.00, in view of the time of the year, the season, what was the visibility, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't very good. It was drizzling. We call it a drizzle. It was dark. Well, I would say that the visibility was bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you again to look at evidence, Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Exhibit 94/2 -- and I'm sorry that you had put it away -- whether this place is there, depicted on the photographs, the place where you encountered the unit. If you can see it there, would you please mark that place.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I could say that that was maybe 3, 4, or 5 metres in front of what photograph 3 depicts. So it's a little bit in front.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So this was the place where you met the unit; is that before or after the crossroads, or at the crossroads?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: It's at the crossroads, towards my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But you can't see these crossroads here?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, you can see it here. You can actually see, where I'm pointing, that's the beginning of the crossroads.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So in that area, a few metres towards your house?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Could you please tell us where your brother's house is, your brother Slavko Sakic? Is that close to your house?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: It's close. It's about 15 metres away from my house. I can indicate that on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, would you please?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Should I show it on the large aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, so that we could see the direction.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: This is my brother's house. (Indicating). This is the crossroads that we were talking about. (Indicating). And that's my house. (Indicating). So this is the road that leads in front of my house towards my brother's house (Indicating). And this section of the road leads towards the garage on the upper part of the house, near the upper part of the house (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that your brother's wife, Jasna Sakic, also came to your house. Do you know who informed her, and when she arrived?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I think she came at the same time that my wife came downstairs, and I think my father probably informed her. My father, Niko Sakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. So another question regarding your testimony from yesterday: You said that you saw Mirjan Santic on the 16th; that he was dead?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That he was brought to your garage and taken home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes. Mirjan Santic. Probably between 10 and 11.00, I'm not sure about the specific time, his body was brought to my garage on the first day of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who took the body home? Who came to get the body?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: His father came from Santici, and a couple of other men went in the direction of Zume and Santici with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would the usher please show the witness Exhibit Number D86/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In the death certificate, it says that the place of death is Santici. And, please, could you read what it says in the attachment on page 3, by the name of Mirjan Santic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have the text. Could it be placed on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Mirjan Franjo Santic, born on the 5th of June, 1956, Vitez. Married, two children. In the military police from the 16th of January 1993. Killed on the 16th of April, 1993, in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In the death certificate it also says that he was killed in Santici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: In the death certificate it says that he was killed in Santici, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Please, this place where you saw him brought, that is to say on the edge of the depression, can one conclude on that basis that he was killed in Santici, or in Pirici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: One cannot conclude it on that basis, because that place is not Santici. That place is Pirici. The border between Pirici and Ahmici, rather.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know the place where he was killed, or did you hear where he was killed?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I heard where he had been killed. I heard that he had been killed by the Kupreskic houses, and the place where I saw him dead for the first time is behind the house of Ivo Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Please, could you also have a look at D87/2. This is the death certificate of Zlatko Ivankovic. Please, what does it say in the death certificate, what is the place of death?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: The place of death says the following: "Ivankovic, Zlatko; day, month and hour of death, 16th of April, 1993; place of death, Ahmici."

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Also, please, could you tell us -- could you have a look at the third page of this document. What does it say underneath Zlatko Ivankovic's picture?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: It also says "Zlatko Ivankovic, born on the 10th of August, 1971, in Travnik; unmarried; in the military police from the 3rd of January 1993; died on the 16th of April 1993 in Vitez."

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Please, you told us that you had seen Mirjan Santic, and that you had heard that Zlatko Ivankovic had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, where was Zlatko Ivankovic killed?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I heard that Zlatko Ivankovic was killed somewhere around the Catholic cemetery; that is to say in the lower part of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And who was killed along with him?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I heard that along with him a man called Zepackic was killed; I don't know his first name. I didn't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who else did you hear about? Who else was killed on that day in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Out of the Croats, I heard that on that day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've given this evidence before. We've heard it all once. We don't need to hear it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the point is that I think that what the witness said yesterday was misunderstood. We heard claims being made today to the effect that these five persons were killed partly in Ahmici, partly in Vitez. The witness claims that he heard that they were killed in Ahmici, and I want this to be stated clearly in the transcript. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has stated it clearly. It's something he heard. We shall have to decide what weight we give to it. And you have --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- produced documents about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Sakic. We will not go into that subject any more. One more thing related to the list that was shown to you by the Prosecutor. This is a list of killed members of the HVO. Do you know whether this is an official document or not? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this, I must admit, nor am I in a position to have any kind of information in this regard, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you say in relation to Mirjan Santic that the information on that list is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I can absolutely state that. I shall repeat once again that I was there, I killed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, interpreter's mistake --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I saw Mirjan Santic who had been killed that day and the date was on one day and this other date was on another day. Again, I'm saying that Mirjan Santic had been killed on the first day of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that your brother, Slavko Sakic, was a member of the anti-aircraft defence, if that is the way we can put it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you say where he was during those three days? Was he, at any point, in Pirici, or rather, Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Absolutely not. These units had their own positions, and it was well known for quite a bit of time where they had been. They were on a position above the Princip factory, and also in the main field, and these were mixed units. I don't know when they separated. So there were Muslims and Croats alike. All the members of the anti-aircraft defence from the previous system.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And did you talk to him about this, where he was after those events?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: He was in Vitez, in the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sakic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I would just like to have admitted into evidence Exhibits 94/2, 95, and 96, respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection? All right. Admitted into evidence. There are no questions for the witness from the Court. Mr. Sakic, thank you for testifying in court. You may now be released. Thank you. I would like to ask the registrar to bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Good day. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Vrebac, would you please introduce yourself to the court?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: I am Zdravko Vrebac, son of Jozo. I was born in Santici. That is also where I live. I was born on the 21st of May, 1966.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you please show us on this aerial photograph where your house is?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes, I will. My house is here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What are the first Croat houses, or, rather, who are your Croat neighbours?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: The first Croat houses are the houses of my kinsmen, the Vrebacs. This is my brother's house, then also the settlement along the road is Vidovici and Santici in the neighbourhood (indicating). That is my immediate neighbourhood around my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And that part of the village, was it primarily Croat?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes, it was primarily Croat, but in the settlement of Zume, where there are new houses, for quite some time there have been some neighbours who are Muslims. And on this side, on the other side of the stream, over here there are a few houses, and here underneath the main road in Donja Zume (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what Muslim families lived in your neighbourhood? Who were your closest neighbours who were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: My closest neighbours were the Podojak family, Reuf Podojak's family. Islam Ahmic. That's it. Then Nesib was here (indicating). I don't know his last name exactly. I think it's Ahmic too. Those houses were built recently most --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You may be seated. Tell us, Mr. Vrebac, what did you do in 1992? Where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: In 1992 I was employed within the SPS factory, within the Sintevit department. I'm talking about electrical maintenance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And how long did you work there? Until when?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: I worked there until the middle of the year, when most of the workers were already on leave, and then I went on leave too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And where did you work after that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: After that I started working in my brother's warehouse. At that time he had a company called Trgogrozd, and it exists to the present day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And where is this warehouse, in Vitez or in Santici?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: The warehouse is in Santici, and that is the wholesale department, whereas the retail was in Novi Travnik, in Bare, and in the Vitezanka building in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, in 1992 did you take part in the village guards?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. From time to time, yes. Since I was employed by my brother, as I already said, so when I had time and -- yeah, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And tell me, these village guards, were they organised in your part of the village in some official way or was this an unofficial duty? How did you perceive this?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Guard duty was not compulsory. It was organised by -- by the villagers themselves, because at that time there were shortages and nobody had any work, and there were certain groups of people who were -- how should I put this -- involved in certain criminal actions such as car thefts and stealing other people's property in general.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you have any weapons at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: No. No. At that time I did not have any weapons. We had weapons at the warehouse. The goods that were in the warehouse were very valuable. That is to say that the warehouse had to be guarded during the night, and sometimes I would stand guard there and sometimes one of the workers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So the rifle belonged to the company, is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes. It was used to guard the warehouse itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you receive any monetary compensation for guard duty?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: No. No, not in any sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what about the Muslims in your part of the village? Did they stand guard with you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, together with me. Very often we had the opportunity of patrolling the village in that part of Zume, in our neighbourhood, that is to say, where we lived and where our closest Muslim neighbours did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How long did these joint guards go on in your part of the village?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Well, they went on until the end of October 1992, just before the conflict broke out. That's how long the joint guards went on. And then after the first conflict, I couldn't say exactly -- there was a truce. I couldn't say a truce because we didn't have any quarrel or war between us, but when the tensions were reduced a little bit it seems.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened on the 20th of October of '92 in your part of the village?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: On the 20th of October, in the morning at around 5.00 a.m., I was woken up by a powerful detonation from the direction -- I mean, I knew later that it was from the direction of Zume, Ahmici and so on, but I was woken up, as I said, by this powerful detonation, after which I got dressed, and I went outside to see what had happened, but it was all quiet after that explosion. So I went to Zume, because I thought that maybe someone from the people I would meet would perhaps know something about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where did you find these people that you said that you expected to meet on the road?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Well, I encountered the first people at Ivo Vidovic's house. I met him there, his brother Anto Vidovic, called Satko; Pero Jelic, I think. Well, several people. Five or six people. They told me that they didn't know what was going on, and I heard about the barricade that had been set up the day before at the cemetery in Santici, just below Ahmici, and that that was probably the reason. So from there I went to the depression behind Niko Sakic's house and below Ivo Kupreskic's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So what did you want to see there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: I didn't want to see anything. That place was always a kind of shelter. So from the former system, from the former state it remain as a kind of natural shelter, as a place where during military exercises, manoeuvres of the JNA, the population would go there. The people who lived in those environs, they would go there. So when I got there I saw Mirko Sakic there; Niko Sakic; Milutin Vidovic; Dragan Vidovic, son of Nikica; and also the people who lived close by and their families.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: These were people who had homes nearby; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So could you please tell us if anything was happening there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Well, nothing was happening at that time. It was maybe at about 6.00 in the morning or 6.30. At that time, around 6.30, we heard a lot of firing from the direction of the cemetery and the elementary school, from that area, as much as you can determine the place from the depression.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was -- did you only hear artillery or were there any other detonations from mortars perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: No, not more powerful weapons. I think it was just firing from artillery weapons, as much as I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And you said that you heard firing from the direction of the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So the only shooting that you heard came from that direction?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this is a good time we can go on break, since all the preparations have been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Vrebac, you mentioned the shooting from the direction of the cemetery and that there was no other shooting, according to your impression. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So what happened after that? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: After that we climbed up a little higher out of the depression so that we could see what was going on, as much as we dared, because we were afraid. And then I saw in front of the house of Ivo Kupreskic, I saw Mirjan Kupreskic, Zoran and Ivica Kupreskic. They were standing there. I could see that they were really afraid, because their families remained in their houses. So Milutin Vidovic and I, and Dragan Vidovic, son of Nikica, ran up to them and from there up to their houses. I ran up to Mica's house, the house of Mirjan Kupreskic , and I took one of his children, he took the other child, and also his wife, and Zoran, with Milutin and Dragan. So we took the children over to Ivo Kupreskic's house. And it was my impression then, and as far as I can remember now, it was terrible, because bullets were whizzing all around us, a lot of bullets, and since we didn't have any kind of experience, we were very scared. And we took the children to the shelter in my sister and brother-in-law's house, Jelena and Dragan Trajanovski. Then we came back to the depression and we stayed there throughout the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you please indicate on the map where this shelter is, the shelter of Jelena Trajanovski?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes. The shelter is right here (indicating), across from my house. So it's in the house of my sister and my brother-in-law. That's where the shelter is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where is your house in relation to that shelter?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: It's directly across (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you said that that was your -- the house of Jelena Trajanovski and her husband. What was her husband's name?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Dragan Trajanovski.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was there any talk in the village that that was the Vrebac house?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Well, it was built on the land which belonged to my father, so all -- everybody in the village, they don't know our family affairs, so the usual name for it was "the house of Vrebac," "Vrebac's house."

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What is your father's name?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: My father's name is Jozo Vrebac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At that time, during the first conflict in '92, was your sister and her husband there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: No. They were working in Germany, in Langefeld, to be precise, and at that time they hadn't even been back to visit us for three years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After that, did they come back? Were they there in '93? In Santici?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: No. From '89 up until '97, they never came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who opened that house? You said you placed Zoran and Mirjan's family in there.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Well, my father opened it. He has keys of the whole house, and also from the shelter. It's an improvised shelter which is located in the basement, in the cellar of the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was that house used as a shelter, usually?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes. In '92, already, as soon as the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina started, with the attack of the Yugoslav army, when the bombardments of those neighbouring towns began, and wider, there was a lot of fear from air attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What other house in that area was used as a shelter? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Each house that had a cellar; or if it had, for example, two floors, two concrete floors. So any house that was built of strong material.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Could you please indicate on the aerial photographs your house, the house of your father, and also the shelter in the house of Jelena Trajanovski.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would the usher please take the map to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D97/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you indicate with a marker where the house of your father is?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: This is my father's house. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And your sister's house?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: That's my sister's house. (Marks).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And also could you please indicate where the house of Milutin Vidovic is.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Also could you mark your father's house with the letter "A," the house of your sister with the letter "B," the house of Milutin Vidovic with the letter "C"; and if you know where the house of Niko Vidovic is -- do you know --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Which Niko Vidovic? There are two Niko Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The house of Niko Vidovic which was used as a shelter. If you know; if you don't know, then we won't indicate it.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: I'm not sure which house. I know where -- its location, but I don't know which house it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Okay. Then these two markings are sufficient. Could you please indicate where are the warehouses that you mentioned earlier. That was your brother's property?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you return after you took the Kupreskics to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I came back to the depression that I mentioned, where we all were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did Zoran and Mirjan go with you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see that Muslims were leaving the village? Did you notice that from the place where you were?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Well, from the place where we were, I couldn't see something like that. But later I heard that they had left the area of Ahmici, lower Ahmici. But I couldn't see that from the area around my house. And then from there, nobody left.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did the families of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic stay in the shelter in your sister's house?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: No. They stayed there for some time; I don't know exactly how long. After a while, they went to Mirjan and Zoran's sister -- her name was Zorica Rajic -- which is deeper inside Santici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know whether their families stayed there for some time, or did they come back on the same day?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: No, nobody came back on the same day. As far as I can remember, after three or four days, the population was beginning to come back to Ahmici. And then when they came back, the Muslim population of Ahmici, then also the Kupreskic families came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What time did the shooting stop on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: When? The shooting stopped at around 3 or 4 p.m. I can't say exactly when, because it waned a little bit, and then it stopped completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So what happened in the region of those three villages after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: After the conflict itself, people -- more prominent people from those hamlets of ours, Muslims and Croats -- tried to calm down the tensions which were caused by the conflict. Nothing important happened except the agreement on the return of everybody to Ahmici, to their homes. Naturally everybody tried to calm down the situation. We were all taken by surprise by it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were there any incidents in the village between the first and the second conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, but there were some times -- because the tensions remained high, regardless of the good will of the locals to have the situation calm down, the trust was up in the air. There were some alerts, and we went to the shelter -- I can't say frequently, but several times. And not everybody went. But there were reports that from some certain region there would be an attack by the Muslims, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did the Muslims ever go to the shelter? Do you know of such occurrences? Did they receive this kind of information?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How much do you actually know about this, what was going on in Ahmici after the conflict, in view of the fact that Santici, the part that you were in, is predominantly Croat?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Well, I know as much as my father could tell me: Namely, my father went to one meeting, or several meetings, perhaps, at this time, immediately after the conflict. I don't know exactly where this meeting was held, or these several meetings were held. However, from what he told me, I know that every possible effort was made to alleviate the situation and to go back to the situation that was before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who did you socialise with from Ahmici -- or Pirici, rather; who was your friend there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Well, I had many friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who were you closest to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: I was closest to Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic, because of the rehearsals we had all the time at the cultural society in Vitez. Also Fahrudin Ahmic was with us, and I can say in all fairness that he was with us non-stop. And this was my immediate circle of friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what about the relations between you and Mirjan, Zoran and Fahran Ahmic; did they change after the conflict in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: No. No. As a matter of fact, I think that after this conflict we actually became closer. I can't really explain this. Nothing substantial changed in our relationship, in our relations among these friends. I mentioned that we went to rehearsals practically every other day, and there were quite a few other Muslims who danced with us. And no, there was no tension or distrust whatsoever that could be felt there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what did you do -- I'm sorry. I'm sorry, one question before that: Where was your brother during the first conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: During the first conflict, my brother was taken prisoner by the Muslims at Opara, near Novi Travnik. I don't know. For some six or seven days he was held prisoner, and his goods and trucks were taken away, those that he was taking from Herzegovina to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know the day when he was taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: I think that it was the 15th of October, in the evening -- no, no. No, on the 19th, the day before the conflict. The day before the first conflict in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In the area of Novi Travnik, were there any conflicts immediately before this conflict in Ahmici? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know about that. There were conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Between who?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Between Croats and Muslims. I think it was some kind of a gasoline station that was involved, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were there any dead people at the time? Was anybody killed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: That, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And do you know whether these conflicts were between the Muslims and the Croats as neighbours, or were they conflicts between the HVO army and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: I think that it was between the HVO and the BH army. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you ever find out what the main reason for the conflict in Ahmici was on the 20th of October?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes. I found out that the main reason was the placement of the roadblock by the Muslims by the cemetery, by the Catholic cemetery, between Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And do you know who took part in this conflict, and whether the Croats from Ahmici and these neighbouring villages, did they take part in this conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: I know for sure that the local Croats did not take part in this conflict. And I know that at that time, the new shift for Jajce passed by that roadblock, because there was heavy fighting in Jajce at the time. I think it was a unit from Kiseljak that was passing by there, and that they were supposed to relieve someone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Out of the people that you saw that day in the depression and who were with you on the 20th of October, did anybody shoot?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So tell us, what did you do before the second conflict, in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Before the second conflict -- that is to say between the first and second conflicts -- I continued to work in the warehouse of the Trgogrozd company. And, as I said, every other day or every third day we had rehearsals at the cultural society of Vitez. And quite often in the evening we would play in the orchestra. And there would be parties, wedding parties. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you do that professionally?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: In the cultural society, we worked as one does work in a cultural society. That is where all the enthusiasm of the people involved is manifested; that is to say, there is no compensation or anything. When Mica -- I mean Mirjan Kupreskic and I and Fahrudin Ahmic, we agreed in principle with the head of the cultural society that we would get some kind of per diems, because we were responsible for the rehearsals. And as regards the parties and other such things, we did charge for that, as much as you could really charge anyone, because there was very little money available.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you at that time open a cafe in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Actually, after the New Year. I don't know. Five or six days. At the crossroads, the main street, and at that time I think it was called the Tito road, and the main road leading into that part of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what did you do on the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, 1993 I worked just like any other day. That is to say, I had various things to do. In connection with my cafe, I went to get my supplies. That was it. Nothing special really, just like the previous days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you saw Mirjan Kupreskic that day?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where was he working at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: At that time he had transferred to Vitez. A week before that he went to work in the Vitezanka building, and he went to work there from this PP Sutra company where he worked, from the warehouse in Ahmici. That is to say, that is when this other retail was opened, and that is where I got most of my supplies. I also got some supplies in other places.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I already asked you whether you saw him that day.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, at the usual time, around noon, 12.00. When I went out to get my supplies, that is when I would see him, and I would buy these supplies and we would chat. We chatted about the rehearsals that were to be held at the cultural society. So this was just chatting, just like any other day, and we liked to be with one another for as long as possible, as much as work permitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see him again on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes. Every day when he would finish his work, that is to say after 5.00 because working hours were until 5.00 at his retail store, and then he would stop by and see me, and then we talked whether we would go straight to the rehearsal, or stay at the cafe or go straight home. So that's what we did every day. He came that day too, between 5.00 and 5.30, that is to say, after the time it took to reach my place, and we were sitting there in good company, may I say. And the cafe worked well, because we socialised. I mean, we -- from the cultural society there were a lot of them who would drop by.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How long did working hours go on otherwise? I mean, of cafes in Vitez at that time.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Well, at that time, like throughout the war, all cafes had shortened working hours. In the evening they would work until 9.00 or 10.00 p.m., depending on what the police had ordered, and also the town municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How long did you work that day?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: That day, around 6.00 p.m. or 6.30, we received orders orally from a policeman that we were supposed to close up the cafe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did that happen otherwise, that they would close down a cafe or a shop?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes, it would happen. I can't say that it happened very often, but it wasn't strange, because -- I don't know. It happened a few times.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At that time did you go home, and who did you go home with?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Well, we didn't go out immediately, because we stayed on a bit longer, and then only when the policeman had warned us for a second time we had to close down. Then we went to my house -- or, rather, to Slavko Vrebac's house. We were going there with -- with his daughter Ivana Vrebac, because she had a car, because my car was being serviced that day, that day when I got the supplies, so she gave us a lift.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you and Mirjan went together, you left the cafe with that girl; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and with my cousin Zarko Verbac and Marin Pesa. I think there was about four or five of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you go home then?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: We parted there, all of us, but I just stopped by to see my cousin, Slavko Vrebac and his family, and we stayed there for, I don't know how long, perhaps until 8.00, 8.00 or 9.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And where did Mirjan Kupreskic go; do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Mirjan went to his house from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On that day, since you were in Vitez in your own cafe, and since there were people who were there who came to the cafe and the police were there and you said that they closed it earlier, did you receive any information as to what would happen on the next day?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: No. On that day we didn't know anything. We just sat there as usual. In my cafe there was Zinka Ibrakovic, a Muslim who was a waitress there, and Edin Sabanovic was sitting together with us before we went home. He was a great friend of mine. Then Islam, Haris, Tudzo. We mixed, the Croats and the Muslims, naturally. We did not separate one from the other. No one knew a thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what happened on the morning of the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: In the morning I was awakened by my father. I think around 5.00, perhaps a bit before that. He woke me up and he said that I should get up and get dressed, and that there was something wrong, because people were coming to the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That is to say that he awakened you because people were coming to what shelter?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: My sister's shelter, my sister Jelena's shelter, and it's marked with a letter "B" on this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did he tell you what was going on in addition to the people coming in? Did he know what it was all about?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: No. No. He didn't say anything. And I can tell you that at that time it wasn't really a strange situation for us. As I said previously, sometimes this would happen due to some kind of misinformation or whatever, people from certain hamlets would come there to the shelter. So we could not have assumed that there would be a conflict at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what did you do then? Where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: I went to the Trgogrozd's warehouse, and I went to see what the guard was doing there, because my brother was away at that time too. He was in Split getting the goods that he was supposed to bring in the next day, and the day after that, depending on what the traffic was like, especially on the Road of Salvation. So I went there and saw the guard who was guarding the warehouse, and I stayed there with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What did you hear and at what time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Perhaps half an hour later, that is to say, around 5.30 in the morning, we heard terrible shooting from the direction of Ahmici. At that time we were taken by surprise too. How come? We didn't know what was going on. We tried to climb up the steps further up, because this warehouse is near a hill, so you can go up. So we tried to see what was going on, but then since there were bullets flying all over it wasn't really a thing that you should do, and we were afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who was in the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: The guard was there, Ivan Plavcic, who had already been working there for some ten days or so, precisely as a guard because of these long trips that my brother had to take in order to get these supplies that he needed. Somebody had to be there all the time, because I had commitments of my own. I could not be there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That is to say that you were there with that guard; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You heard shooting. Did you see anything? You said that you tried to see -- what did you see from the direction of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Well, yes. Half an hour after the shooting started we were a bit encouraged, so we went upstairs and we saw from Ahmici -- we saw big pillars of smoke, and I told Ivan then that I supposed that Zoran's and Mirjan's houses were on fire, or one of them, in that area. That's what it looked like then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What kind of fire did you hear, small-arms fire or heavy gunfire, and from what direction?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Small-arms fire mostly. Perhaps some smaller detonations. Perhaps these were hand grenades or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Around 6.30 or 7.00, I don't know when, I agreed with the guard that we leave the warehouse after all, because it was not exactly advisable to stay there in view of its position. On the other hand, it's a big building and perhaps it would attract someone. Therefore, I called my brother around 6.30, and he was in Split at the time, and I told him that there was heavy shooting and that I saw these pillars of smoke in the direction of those houses, and I told him to wait a bit because he was supposed to leave, and I told him to wait and I was afraid for him. I was afraid that he would be taken prisoner again or something. Then we went to the house of Slavko Vrebac. Just as we moved from the warehouse, some 30 metres or so, behind us we heard a strong detonation and we fell. Of course, we ran away from there, we went to the house of my uncle, Marko Vrebac, but after that we saw where a mortar shell had fallen. We recognised it by its tip.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: By its tail?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, by the stabiliser that it has. We saw that only later. We went to that place, and we were there with these kinsmen of mine, Vlado Vrebac, Zarko Vrebac, Marko Vrebac. They were all at home. Those are my uncle and cousins.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you go to your house, to your father, Jozo Vrebac?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Not right away. I went there maybe at around 9.00, but first I took some food supplies from the warehouse in order to take that up there, because I could see these people who arrived at the shelter in the morning. So when I got there, I saw that the shelter was full of people, too many people. More than it could hold. There was a large number of people. So I saw that I didn't take enough food. I expected to only find a couple of families there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How many people were there, in your estimate, when you got there? Can you tell us approximately?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: About a hundred people approximately, perhaps more. That's what I think. I don't know really what -- how big the basement was but it was overcrowded. I think it was about a hundred people or more.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic that day?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes. When I was leaving the house, when I left the food, mostly for the children who were there, and the women, I met them, the two of them, Mirjan and Zoran, and Mirko Sarkic also came with them. They came because their families were there. Mirjan Kupreskic's family was there. Zoran's family was in the house of Milutin Vidovic. That's what he told me at that time. So that's when we met. We talked about everything that was happening. We were all shocked and surprised by what was going on. So Mica, Mirjan Kupreskic, told me then that they met, when they were coming back from the Pudza houses, from the depression, they saw Satko, Anto Vidovic, and he told them that he was in tears too, that he was with the mother of Fahrudin Ahmic, our friend, and she had told him that Fahran was killed. I will cannot describe to you the shock that we were in when we found out about that. We were with that man every day, and we couldn't have assumed that something like that could happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What time was that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: It was between 9.00 and 10.00 in the morning, around that time. Maybe at about 9.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know, did Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic tell you where they were?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes. They said they were behind the house of Niko Sakic, in the same depression that I had talked about earlier. So they were there. That's where they were. At the last houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see them again on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: No, I didn't meet them any more that day, because I went back to the warehouse. And I was going back and forth from the warehouse to my cousin's and to the house of Slavko Vrebac, so I was in that area all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you have a gun?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: I did have a gun that day. I took it from the security guard. And then I left it where it usually stays, in the office, in the warehouse, in the office next to the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were there any kind of fighting or combat activities in the region where you were on that day, so in the area between the warehouse and your house and the house of your cousins?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: No. No. But at my father's place, just below his house, where I lived too, the clearing, practically in the garden, a mortar shell fell, we assumed from the direction of Sljibcica or Sivrino Selo, or thereabouts. So that's what my father told me on that day. And then afterwards we saw the traces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were there any combat activities in the region of Sljibcica and Sivrino Selo?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes. By the mortar shell in the morning, according to that, I think that's where it came from, at the warehouse. Because when they saw the security guard and me coming out of the warehouse, I think that they fired it then. But it's my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who was holding those positions?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Muslims. The BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic in the course of the second or the third day?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Not during the second day. But I saw them on the third day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On the second day, where were you? Could you just tell us briefly?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Well, I stayed in the warehouse; also occasionally I would go to visit my uncle; occasionally I would go to visit my father, to see my family, how they were doing, if they needed anything. Occasionally I would take some food to the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So then on the third day you say you saw Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic; tell us where.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: On the third day, I saw them. At the time, it was noon. When I took goods, there was a lot of -- there were a lot of goods, so I took that with my Citroen car to the shelter in my sister's house, and I gave that for them there. And I wanted to find out how they were doing, because there was constant shooting, and I wanted to know this. So I went to Niko Sakic's house, where I left the car, and I saw them right next to his garage, in that depression. The two of them, Mirko Sakic -- I don't know, there were -- also Grgic was there. I don't know his name. Mirko, something like that. I saw them. They were there. And then Mirjan told me then that we need to go to his house somehow to get the accordion. So we went to his house, and we found that the door had been broken in. There was a lot of -- there were a lot of holes from bullets on the facade of the house. We saw that the door had been ripped open, and everything in the house had been ransacked. The windows were broken, and the door frames -- we could see a bullet that had started a fire in the door frame, but the fire didn't catch on, so nothing was burnt. But the accordion was underneath the bed of one of the children, so we took the accordion, and then he also saw that some things were missing that had belonged to his wife, gold, that these things had been taken. So we had to go back quickly, because it wasn't wise to remain there. So we took the accordion back to the depression. And I placed it in my car and I took it home, so that's where it was until the end of the war, so until the first ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Why did you go to get the accordion? You said there was still shooting in certain parts of the village. Wasn't that dangerous?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Well, why did we go? It was dangerous. But I know what my instrument, my musical instrument, means to me, so I know also what it means to Mirjan, what the accordion means to Mirjan. It's the most valuable material thing that a man could have. I can't even explain the love for a musical instrument. It practically meant a half of his life.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So where was the accordion placed, then? You said --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Well, in my father's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On the third day, were you mobilised? Were you taken to the lines?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: On that day, when I returned the car to the warehouse, in the afternoon, before it got dark, maybe at twilight, three soldiers came to my uncle's house, which is where I came after I left the warehouse. And they found me there, my cousin Vlado, Zarko Vrebac. Marko was also there -- this is my uncle; he is an older man. He is a grandfather. They told us then to get ready -- or to follow them immediately. And they took us to upper Zume, to Marko Livancic's house. And then another two soldiers accompanied us to Pirici, above the Muslim cemetery, but below the forest. And it's called -- the forest is called Barin Gaj, and this is where they placed us. And they gave us a shovel and a pickaxe and told us to start digging.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you say your uncle was with you as well, how old was he?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: He was born in 1924.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: He was taken there with you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: No. No. He stayed in front of his house. He wasn't taken with us. He's a very old man.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you remained on that line where you were brought, and how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: How long?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The whole war?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: No, not the whole war. I remained there for maybe 20 days; maybe a little longer. After that, I went to Vitez, because they came to get me. They needed me to maintain electronic equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know how and when the family of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic went to Vitez, and from where?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: I know that on the 15th day, they left, because I drove them. I had a small minivan, a Volkswagen van, in my warehouse. So Mirjan and Zoran told me that they needed to transfer them up there, because the house of their sister, Ljubica Kupreskic, was empty, because the sister and brother-in-law were in Switzerland working.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This house is in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes, in Vitez. In the -- I don't know which part; it's called Mlakici, next to the high school.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where was Ljubica Kupreskic until then, before she went to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Ljubica Kupreskic was in the house of Pero Santic, I think, Radak. This is across the Lasva. Across the bridge itself, when you go, so the house is close to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And whose wife is Ljubica Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: She's the wife of Mirjan Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So is that where you picked her up?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes. We first picked up Zoran's wife from Milutin's house, and the children, we picked them up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Whose house was she in?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: In the house of Milutin Vidovic. So we picked them up; then we went to the Radaks, across the Lasva, and we picked up Ljubica and the children, and we went across Rijeka in a different road because you couldn't take the main road. So we took a detour because of the snipers on the main road. So it was very risky to use the main road.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did Ljubica Kupreskic -- who was she with in Pero Santic's house?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: She was there with her children. Ankica Kupreskic was there with her children. There was -- there were a lot of people who had to leave their own homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you remember if Ljubica's mother was there with Ljubica?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VREBAC.
utterances.text: Yes. Her mother was very old and very sick, and I remember that my father told me that they pushed her in a wheelbarrow, and that they brought her to the Radak houses in the wheelbarrow, and then from -- they brought her to our shelter also in the same wheelbarrow. So we picked them up, and then we took them to Vitez, where we settled them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm finished with this part. I still have another half an hour for tomorrow, but it's a completely different part. So I would ask that we begin with that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. So we adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 1:25 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 5th day of March, 1999, at 9.00 a.m.
